> **How to read this file.** Section 3 runs the simulation, sections 4 and 5 show the evidence, and section 8 states my selected n. The reusable code lives in `R/functions.R`; this file only calls it.

## 1. Prediction

This one breaks the "identical" part of the CLT. Observation i is a Bernoulli (0 or 1) whose success chance falls steadily from 0.90 for the first observation to 0.50 for the last, like a basketball player getting tired during a game. The observations are still independent, so I predict the CLT still works, but the mean and spread need a new formula because every observation has its own probability. I predict a selected n of about 10 to 15, similar to a Bernoulli with p around 0.7.

## 2. The population

```{r}
#| label: setup
source("R/setup.R")
source("R/functions.R")

make_p <- function(n) seq(from = 0.90, to = 0.50, length.out = n)
generator <- function(n) rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = make_p(n))

n_names  <- as.character(n_values)
mu_n     <- sapply(n_values, function(n) mean(make_p(n)))
sigma_n  <- sapply(n_values, function(n) sqrt(mean(make_p(n) * (1 - make_p(n)))))
names(mu_n) <- n_names
names(sigma_n) <- n_names
```

A sample of size n is a game of n shots. Shot i has success probability p_i, and the p_i are spaced evenly from 0.90 down to 0.50 (the same setup as the teacher's basketball example). The sample mean is the shooting percentage.

Because the p_i differ, the formulas change:

- Mean of the sample mean: the average of the p_i, which is `r round(mu_n["20"], 2)` for a 20-shot game (and 0.70 for every n of 2 or more; the n = 1 sample is just the first shot, p = 0.90).
- Standard error: √(Σ p_i(1 − p_i)) / n. I write this as σ_n/√n, where σ_n = √(average of p_i(1 − p_i)) is the effective standard deviation of one shot at that n. It is about `r round(sigma_n["20"], 3)` for n = 20, and the code below passes it in for every n.

```{r}
#| label: population-plot
#| fig-height: 3
plot(1:20, make_p(20), type = "b", pch = 19, col = "firebrick", ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "shot number", ylab = "probability of a make",
     main = "Non-identical Bernoulli: p falls from 0.90 to 0.50 (n = 20)")
```

## 3. Simulation

For every sample size n in my list (`r min(n_values)` to `r max(n_values)`, `r length(n_values)` sizes), I simulate B = `r format(B, big.mark = ",")` games of n shots and keep each game's shooting percentage. B is the number of repetitions; n is the size of each sample.

```{r}
#| label: simulate
all_means <- simulate_all_n(generator, n_values)
results   <- summarize_means(all_means, mu_n, sigma_n)
results$good <- flag_good(results)
n_star <- smallest_good_n(results)

dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)
write.csv(results, "results/06_nonidentical_bernoulli.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

## 4. Results

Selected sample sizes (the full table of all `r nrow(results)` sizes is saved in `results/06_nonidentical_bernoulli.csv`). `theory_mean` is the average of the p_i and `theory_se` is √(Σ p_i(1 − p_i)) / n:

```{r}
#| label: table
key_n <- sort(unique(c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 100, n_star)))
show  <- results[results$n %in% key_n, c("n", "sim_mean", "theory_mean", "sim_sd",
                                         "theory_se", "sd_ratio", "skewness",
                                         "excess_kurtosis")]
show$passes <- ifelse(results$good[results$n %in% key_n], "yes", "no")
knitr::kable(show, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

## 5. Plots

**Histograms of the sample means**, with the theoretical normal curve N(mean of the p_i, SE) in red. I show the same sample sizes in every analysis (1, 2, 5, 30) plus my selected n. A shooting percentage can only be 0, 1/n, 2/n and so on, so `step = 1` lines the bars up with those values:

```{r}
#| label: histograms
show_n <- sort(unique(c(1, 2, 5, 30, n_star)))
plot_histograms(all_means, show_n, mu_n, sigma_n, "Non-identical Bernoulli", step = 1)
```

**Q–Q plots** (points on the red line = normal):

```{r}
#| label: qqplots
plot_qq(all_means, show_n, "Non-identical Bernoulli")
```

You can try any n yourself in the [Interactive Sampling Distribution Explorer](https://nprodhuturi.github.io/clt-monte-carlo/interactive/explorer.html), which includes this population.

**Diagnostics across every n.** Dashed lines mark my "approximately normal" limits (defined in section 6):

```{r}
#| label: diagnostics
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
plot(results$n, results$skewness, type = "b", pch = 16, cex = 0.6,
     ylim = range(c(results$skewness, -0.25, 0.25)),
     xlab = "n", ylab = "skewness", main = "Skewness of sample means")
abline(h = c(-0.25, 0, 0.25), lty = c(2, 1, 2), col = "firebrick")

plot(results$n, results$excess_kurtosis, type = "b", pch = 16, cex = 0.6,
     ylim = range(c(results$excess_kurtosis, -0.5, 0.5)),
     xlab = "n", ylab = "excess kurtosis", main = "Excess kurtosis")
abline(h = c(-0.5, 0, 0.5), lty = c(2, 1, 2), col = "firebrick")

plot(results$n, results$sd_ratio, type = "b", pch = 16, cex = 0.6,
     ylim = range(c(results$sd_ratio, 0.95, 1.05)),
     xlab = "n", ylab = "simulated SD / theoretical SE", main = "Spread vs. theory")
abline(h = c(0.95, 1, 1.05), lty = c(2, 1, 2), col = "firebrick")
```

**Does changing the probability matter?** The teacher's basketball example asks whether the normal approximation works the same when the probabilities are constant or when they change. To answer it, I run the same simulation for a shooter whose probability is **constant at 0.70** (the average of the changing ones) and compare:

```{r}
#| label: constant-comparison
generator_c  <- function(n) rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = 0.70)
all_means_c  <- simulate_all_n(generator_c, n_values)
results_c    <- summarize_means(all_means_c, 0.70, sqrt(0.70 * 0.30))
results_c$good <- flag_good(results_c)
n_star_c     <- smallest_good_n(results_c)

k <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 12, 15, 20, 30)
compare <- data.frame(
  n = k,
  skew_changing    = results$skewness[results$n %in% k],
  skew_constant    = results_c$skewness[results_c$n %in% k],
  kurt_changing    = results$excess_kurtosis[results$n %in% k],
  kurt_constant    = results_c$excess_kurtosis[results_c$n %in% k]
)
knitr::kable(compare, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

Apart from n = 1 (where the changing version is just the first shot, p = 0.90), the two columns are almost the same at every n. The selected n is `r n_star` for the changing probabilities and `r n_star_c` for the constant 0.70. So the changing probability barely changes how fast the average becomes normal.

**One simulated game**, as in the teacher's example: the red line is the probability of making each shot, and the blue points are what actually happened (1 = made, 0 = missed):

```{r}
#| label: one-game
#| fig-height: 3
shots <- 1:20
p20   <- make_p(20)
made  <- rbinom(20, size = 1, prob = p20)
plot(shots, p20, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "firebrick", ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "shot number", ylab = "probability / outcome",
     main = "Shooting probability decreases with fatigue (one simulated game)")
points(shots, made, pch = 19, col = "steelblue", cex = 1.2)
legend("bottomleft", legend = c("probability of a make", "actual outcome"),
       col = c("firebrick", "steelblue"), pch = 19, bty = "n")
```

## 6. My definition of "approximately normal"

I use the same rule in every analysis. A sample size n counts as approximately normal when **all four** of these hold:

1.  The histogram is bell-shaped and the Q–Q plot is close to the line.
2.  \|skewness\| ≤ 0.25.
3.  \|excess kurtosis\| ≤ 0.5.
4.  The simulated SD is within 5% of the theoretical SE.

My selected n is the smallest n that passes and stays passing for every larger n I tested, so a lucky pass at one n doesn't count. The reasons for each cutoff are in [01_standard_normal.md](01_standard_normal.md). Here the "theoretical SE" is the non-identical one from section 2.

## 7. Interpretation

```{r}
#| label: interpretation
at_star  <- results[results$n == n_star, ]
before   <- results[results$n < n_star, ]
below    <- before[nrow(before), ]
at_one   <- results[results$n == 1, ]
sd_lo    <- min(results$sd_ratio[results$n > 1])
sd_hi    <- max(results$sd_ratio[results$n > 1])
max_mean_err <- max(abs(results$sim_mean - results$theory_mean))
```

- **Shape.** At n = 1 there are only two bars (0 and 1), with most of the weight on 1, so the histogram is lopsided to the left and the Q–Q plot is two flat steps. As n grows the shooting percentages fill in and the picture becomes a bell centered near 0.70, with a slight lean to the left that fades.
- **Mean.** The simulated mean matches the average of the p_i, never missing by more than `r round(max_mean_err, 3)`. Note that this center is 0.70, not 0.50 or 0.90, because the probabilities change during the game.
- **Spread.** For n of 2 or more, the simulated SD divided by the non-identical theoretical SE stays between `r round(sd_lo, 3)` and `r round(sd_hi, 3)`. If I had wrongly used the formula for identical shots with p = 0.70, the spread would have been off, because shots with p near 0.5 vary more than shots with p near 0.9.
- **Skewness.** At n = 1 the skewness is `r round(at_one$skewness, 2)` (a single 0.90 shot), and it falls as n grows. At n = 2 both skewness and kurtosis fail. By n = 5 the kurtosis is already fine but the skewness (`r round(results$skewness[results$n == 5], 2)`) still fails, so skewness is the last check to pass.

**CLT assumptions.** The observations are independent with finite variance, but **not identically distributed**. The CLT still works here because no single observation dominates the sum (all the variances are similar and bounded). So "identical" is not strictly needed; what matters is independence and that no one term is too large.

**Limitations / surprises.** The surprise is that a changing probability does not slow the CLT down much: the comparison in section 5 shows the result (n = `r n_star`) is almost the same as for a constant 0.70 (n = `r n_star_c`). The caveat is that I have to use the right mean and SE, since the identical-shot formulas would be wrong. Also, if the shots were not independent (a hot streak, for example), this would no longer be a CLT situation.

## 8. Selected n and justification

| **Final answer: n = `r n_star`** |
|:--------------------------------:|

$$\boxed{n = `r n_star`}$$

- **Evidence at n = `r n_star`.** Skewness `r round(at_star$skewness, 3)` (limit ±0.25), excess kurtosis `r round(at_star$excess_kurtosis, 3)` (limit ±0.5), and SD ratio `r round(at_star$sd_ratio, 3)` (limit 1 ± 0.05). The histogram follows the normal curve, and the Q–Q plot follows the line apart from small steps caused by the discrete values.
- **Why not smaller.** At n = `r below$n`, the skewness is `r round(below$skewness, 3)` and the excess kurtosis is `r round(below$excess_kurtosis, 3)`, so at least one check fails.
- **It stays passing.** Every larger n I tested, up to n = `r max(n_values)`, also passes.
- **Is the number 30?** No. This population needs about n = `r n_star`, so 30 is `r round(30 / n_star, 1)` times what is needed.
